facts.claim: Adult label maximums and drug content per US dental cartridge. Lidocaine 2% with epinephrine 1:100,000 or 1:50,000: 34 mg per 1.7 mL (20 mg/mL); not over 7 mg/kg (3.2 mg/lb), and keep the total below 500 mg in a healthy adult. Articaine 4% with epinephrine 1:100,000 or 1:200,000: 68 mg per 1.7 mL (40 mg/mL); 7 mg/kg, with no absolute mg cap on the label. Mepivacaine 3% plain (51 mg per 1.7 mL) and 2% with levonordefrin 1:20,000 (34 mg per 1.7 mL): up to 3 mg/lb (6.6 mg/kg), never more than 400 mg per sitting. Prilocaine 4% plain or with epinephrine 1:200,000: 72 mg per 1.8 mL; 8 mg/kg (4 mg/lb) under 70 kg (150 lb), 600 mg (8 cartridges) at 70 kg or more. Bupivacaine 0.5% with epinephrine 1:200,000: 9 mg per 1.8 mL; ordinarily no more than 90 mg per sitting in a healthy adult (ten 1.8 mL cartridges).
facts.conditions: US dental lidocaine and mepivacaine cartridges are labeled 1.7 mL; prilocaine and bupivacaine 1.8 mL. Items that say '1.8 mL of 2% lidocaine = 36 mg' follow an older convention: prefer the label's 34 mg per 1.7 mL, or state the volume in the stem.

facts.claim: Early CNS toxicity signs: restlessness, anxiety, tinnitus, dizziness, blurred vision, tremors, depression or drowsiness. AAPD: toxicity is biphasic (excitation then depression); early subjective signs are dizziness, anxiety, confusion, then diplopia, tinnitus, drowsiness, circumoral numbness/tingling; objective signs are muscle twitching, tremor, talkativeness, slowed speech, shivering, then a generalized tonic-clonic seizure (the classic overdose reaction), loss of consciousness and respiratory arrest. Cardiovascular: HR and BP may rise at first (epinephrine), then vasodilation, myocardial depression, falling BP, bradycardia and arrest. Most reactions come during the injection or within 5-10 minutes.

cites.quote: Restlessness, anxiety, tinnitus, dizziness, blurred vision, tremors, depression, or drowsiness may be early warning signs of central nervous system toxicity.
Most adverse drug reactions develop either during the injection or within 5 to 10 minutes.

facts.claim: Toxicity management: stop the anesthetic, airway and ventilation first; anticonvulsant if seizures persist despite ventilation; CPR if arrest. AAPD: early IV lipid emulsion is a priority in potentially serious LAST; activate EMS by severity. Prevention: aspirate, inject slowly, calculate the maximum by weight. Small dental doses can cause toxic reactions through intra-arterial injection with retrograde flow to the brain.

cites.quote: Early treatment with intravenous lipid emulsion therapy is a priority in potentially serious cases of LAST.
These reactions may be due to intra-arterial injection of the local anesthetic with retrograde flow to the cerebral circulation.

facts.claim: Methemoglobinemia: any LA can cause it; higher risk with G6PD deficiency, congenital or idiopathic methemoglobinemia, cardiac or pulmonary compromise, infants under 6 months, and other oxidizing drugs. Signs: cyanosis (gray/blue skin, nail beds, lips), abnormally colored blood, headache, tachycardia, shortness of breath, fatigue; can appear immediately or hours later. Treat: stop the drug, oxygen, and for severe cases IV methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg over 5 minutes, exchange transfusion or hyperbaric oxygen. Prilocaine's metabolite o-toluidine forms methemoglobin; prilocaine is contraindicated in congenital or idiopathic methemoglobinemia. AAPD: benzocaine contraindicated with a history of methemoglobinemia and under age 2; prilocaine relatively contraindicated in G6PD deficiency, sickle cell anemia, anemia, very young patients or hypoxia.
facts.conditions: The methylene blue dose (1-2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes) is in the label text but not yet quoted.

facts.claim: Cardiac dose ceiling: the healthy-adult maximum of epinephrine in dental anesthesia is commonly given as 0.2 mg, lowered to 0.04 mg for patients with significant cardiovascular disease (ASA III-IV). 0.04 mg = about 2 cartridges of 1:100,000 (0.017-0.018 mg each; see LA-3, LA-6) or about 4 cartridges of 1:200,000. Keep it as "0.04 mg"; the cartridge count is a derived teaching number.
facts.conditions: 0.04 mg is about 2 cartridges of 1:100,000 (derived teaching number; VC-8 gives ADA's own conversion).

cites.quote: The maximum dose of epinephrine in local anaesthesia for a healthy subject is 0.2 mg, though this can be lowered to 0.04 mg if patient has severe cardiovascular disease (ASA III and IV)

facts.claim: The same review concluded that up to 4 cartridges of lidocaine with epinephrine 1:100,000 seemed relatively safe in cardiovascular-compromised patients, that most arrhythmias seen were clinically insignificant, and that ECG monitoring should be considered at higher doses. AHA/ADA position cited there: no contraindication to vasoconstrictor if given carefully with aspiration (Background).
facts.conditions: Most arrhythmias seen were clinically insignificant (same conclusions). ECG monitoring at higher doses is the review's suggestion.

facts.claim: Label interactions (epinephrine-containing dental LAs): with MAO inhibitors, nonselective beta-blockers or tricyclic antidepressants, severe prolonged hypertension can occur; phenothiazines and butyrophenones may reduce or reverse epinephrine's pressor effect; avoid concurrent use, or monitor closely if unavoidable. Xylocaine Dental: with a beta-blocker (propranolol, timolol), dose-dependent hypertension and bradycardia with possible heart block. Vasopressors plus ergot-type oxytocics: severe persistent hypertension or stroke.

cites.quote: monoamine oxidase inhibitors, nonselective beta-adrenergic antagonists, or tricyclic antidepressants may produce severe, prolonged hypertension. Phenothiazines and butyrophenones may reduce or reverse the pressor effect of epinephrine.

facts.claim: Mechanism of the nonselective beta-blocker interaction: with beta-2 vasodilation blocked, epinephrine's alpha-1 vasoconstriction is unopposed, so BP rises and a reflex bradycardia follows. Cardioselective (beta-1) blockers such as metoprolol and atenolol are not named in the labels' warning.
facts.conditions: The mechanism (unopposed alpha-1 with beta-2 blocked, reflex bradycardia) is a teaching paraphrase; only the label effect is sourced.

facts.claim: TCAs and SNRIs block norepinephrine reuptake, so injected epinephrine and especially levonordefrin (mainly alpha effects, so the effect is mostly on BP) can have exaggerated, prolonged effects; minimize the epinephrine dose and inject slowly. Amphetamines (e.g., Adderall) and atomoxetine share this concern; SSRIs, trazodone, mirtazapine and bupropion do not have significant epinephrine interactions.

facts.claim: MAOIs: pharmacologically no interaction with direct-acting agents like epinephrine is expected, but the labels still advise caution (VC-3); the dangerous MAOI interaction is with indirect-acting sympathomimetics (ephedrine, pseudoephedrine), which can cause hypertensive crisis and are contraindicated. Don't stop an MAOI without the psychiatrist.

facts.claim: Cocaine and other stimulants: they are sympathomimetic, so epinephrine-containing LA, epinephrine retraction cord and nitrous oxide may be contraindicated in a patient who has just used cocaine; elective care can usually be done 24 hours after the last stimulant (cocaine, crack, amphetamine) use. Methamphetamine acts for about 8-12 hours.

facts.claim: The OraVerse label says its effect on reversal of local anesthesia of the teeth, mandible, and maxilla has not been assessed.

facts.claim: During ADA minimal sedation, continuously assess level of consciousness and pulse-oximetry oxygen saturation; observe chest movement and verify respirations, with blood pressure and heart rate evaluated before and after treatment and intraoperatively as needed.

facts.claim: For ADA moderate sedation, the qualified dentist must remain in the operatory and continuously assess consciousness and oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry; ventilation must be monitored with end-tidal CO2 unless precluded or invalidated.

facts.claim: If a patient enters a deeper sedation level than the dentist is qualified to provide, ADA directs the dentist to stop dental treatment until the patient returns to the intended level.

facts.claim: AAPD reports that nitrous oxide titration can begin with 100% oxygen for 1–2 minutes followed by 10% nitrous-oxide increments; 30–40% usually achieves analgesia/anxiolysis, and concentration should not routinely exceed 50%.

facts.claim: ADA minimal sedation is a pharmacologically produced minimally depressed level of consciousness in which the patient retains a normal response to verbal command, can independently maintain an airway, and has unaffected ventilatory and cardiovascular function.

facts.claim: ADA moderate sedation is drug-induced depression of consciousness with purposeful response to verbal command, alone or with light tactile stimulation; no airway intervention is required, spontaneous ventilation is adequate, and cardiovascular function is usually maintained.

facts.claim: Nitrous oxide/oxygen combined with one or more sedative agents may produce minimal, moderate, deep sedation, or general anesthesia; classify and monitor according to the actual depth reached.

facts.claim: Adding a vasoconstrictor such as epinephrine or levonordefrin slows local-anesthetic absorption into the bloodstream and can lengthen local duration at the target site.

facts.claim: Epinephrine-containing local-anesthetic solutions are more acidic to prolong vasoconstrictor shelf life; this acidity may increase injection pain and may slow anesthetic onset.
